questions.q: A brewer pitches a bottom-fermenting yeast for a cool, slow, clean ferment. Which species does the Court name for it?
questions.exp: Lager yeast is Saccharomyces pastorianus, which the Court sets cool and slow at 48 to 55°F (9 to 13°C); ale yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, warm and fast. Saccharomyces bayanus is a wine yeast often used for sparkling wine, and Brettanomyces a wild yeast of lambic and some sour beers.

questions.q: Ale yeast ferments warm and fast. At what temperature does the Court place that fermentation?
questions.exp: The Court places ale fermentation at 68 to 72°F (20 to 22°C), where top fermenting Saccharomyces cerevisiae throws fruity, spicy esters. Lager ferments cool and slow at 48 to 55°F (9 to 13°C), and the near freezing rest that follows it is lagering.

questions.q: Cascade and Centennial are two of the Court's three American hop varieties. Which is the third?
questions.exp: The Court's American hops are Cascade, Centennial and Citra, bred for grapefruit, pine and tropical fruit. Saaz, Hallertau and Tettnang are its European hops, the spicy, herbal noble varieties of Bohemia and southern Germany.

questions.q: In which ancient land, says the Court's history of beer, did nomadic peoples settle down to farm and grow grain for both bread and beer?
questions.exp: The Court opens beer's history in Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates, where people who had lived by hunting and gathering settled to farm and grew grain for bread and beer. Its wider point is that each classic style belongs to a particular time and place.

questions.q: Which of the Court's named beer glasses is the traditional pour for a cloudy Bavarian wheat beer?
questions.exp: The tall weizen glass, narrow at the foot and swelling towards the rim, holds the big, fluffy head of a Hefeweizen and shows off its haze. The Court's other named glasses are the pint, the mug, the tulip and the tall, tapered pilsner.

questions.q: Which of the Court's beer glasses has a rounded bowl that narrows and then flares out at the lip, holding the head and gathering aroma?
questions.exp: The tulip's rounded bowl and flared lip hold a generous head and gather aroma, so it suits strong Belgian ales and aromatic IPAs. The Court asks a candidate to recognise the name and shape of the pint, mug, tulip, pilsner and weizen glass, each polished clean.

questions.q: The Court names four principles for pairing beer with food: sweetness from malt, bitterness from hops and a generally low alcohol are three. What is the fourth?
questions.exp: Carbonation completes the Court's four principles. The bubbles scrub fat and salt from the palate, which is why a crisp lager or a saison flatters fried food and rich cheese, while the modest alcohol keeps beer from swamping a dish.

questions.q: A private dining event expects 200 guests, and 40 per cent of them will order one 16 ounce pint of a beer sold only in quarter barrel kegs of 992 ounces (29.3 litres). How many quarter barrel kegs must be ordered?
questions.exp: Work it in the Court's three steps: 40 per cent of 200 guests is 80 pints; 80 pints at 16 ounces is 1,280 ounces; and 1,280 divided by the 992 ounces in a quarter barrel is about 1.3, so two kegs must be ordered, since part of a keg cannot be bought.

questions.q: Craft beer spec sheets print a bitterness figure under the letters IBU. What do those three letters stand for?
questions.exp: IBU stands for International Bitterness Units, a laboratory measure of dissolved hop acids: the higher the figure, the more bitter the beer, though malt sweetness can mask a high reading. ABV, the other figure on the Court's list, is alcohol by volume.

questions.q: Brewed in Dublin since 1759, Guinness is a producer a sommelier can name for which of the Court's beer styles?
questions.exp: Guinness is the benchmark Irish Dry Stout, black from roasted barley yet light in body and alcohol, and poured on a nitrogen mix for its creamy head. The Court asks a candidate to name at least two producers for each of its ten styles, from European Pale Lager to Sour Beer.

questions.q: Crushed malt rests in water at about 65°C while its own enzymes turn starch into fermentable sugar. Which of the Court's production steps is that?
questions.exp: Mashing is the first of the Court's two Certified production steps: the enzymes woken by germination convert starch to sugar, and the sweet liquid drawn off is the wort. Boiling follows, sterilising the wort and drawing bitterness from the hops; kilning belongs to malting, and lagering comes after fermentation.
